transcript.content: Hello, and welcome. I'm Dr. [Name], a psychiatrist. What brings you in to see me today?

Hello, Doctor. Well, what brings me in is... it's my eating. Once I start eating those comfort foods, I just tell myself, 'Maria, that is enough,' but my hand still goes back to the pot. It's like I just can’t make myself stop.
When you're eating these comfort foods and can't stop, do you feel like you're eating much larger amounts than most people would eat in a similar situation?

Yes, I do. Some afternoons, like after I get back from choir or if I've been working out in the garden, I'll fix myself a plate of rice and beans or maybe some chicken stew. But then I just keep going back for more. Before I know it, I've eaten enough for two or three meals... so, yes, it is definitely a lot more than what most people would eat at one time.
After these episodes where you eat so much, do you feel upset, guilty, or ashamed about what you've eaten?

Yes, I do. Afterward... I just feel ashamed, and sad. It's hard because, well, making that kind of food used to mean family and caring. And now it feels like I've turned it into something I have to hide from the people at my church.
After you eat all that food and feel ashamed, do you do anything to try to make up for it — like exercising a lot, fasting the next day, or anything else to compensate?

No, I don't do anything like that. I just... I feel bad about it, but I don't try to starve myself the next day or go out and run or anything. I just go on with my day, feeling heavy and upset with myself.
